turns.question: We have got the acidity, conductivity, oxygen and redox sensors all hanging off one instrument and they are all due at once. Does it matter what order I work through them in, or can I just start anywhere?
turns.answer: The USGS field‑measurement guidance recommends a specific installation order for multiple probes: the pH probe should be placed downstream of the conductivity probe【6†"For a system in which individual sensors are to be installed in the chamber, install the pH sensor downstream from the conductivity sensor."】. Apart from that placement rule, you can take the readings in any sequence as long as each sensor is calibrated and allowed to equilibrate to the water temperature before recording.

A conductivity probe is a very simple device. It is just two conductors with a fixed surface
area at a fixed distance from each other. This distance and surface area is known as the
conductivity cell. The cells distance and surface area is quantified as the conductivity cells
K constant.
How often do you need to
recalibrate a conductivity probe?
Conductivity probes work by measuring the electrical current of the water between two
graphite plates. The plates do not go bad, or change, so recalibration is not necessary. After
the first calibration your conductivity probe is good to go.

ORP stands for oxidation/reduction potential. Oxidation is the loss of electrons and
reduction is the gain of electrons. The output of the probe is represented in millivolts and
can be positive or negative.
Just like a pH probe measures hydrogen ion activity in a liquid; an ORP probe measures
electron activity in a liquid. The ORP readings represents how strongly electrons are
transferred to or from substances in a liquid. Keeping in mind that the readings do not
indicate the amount of electrons available for transfer.

An ORP probe is a passive device that detects a current generated from the oxidation or
reduction chemical substances in water. This current (which can be positive or negative)
is very weak and cannot be detected with a multimeter, or an analog to digital converter.
How often do you need
to recalibrate an ORP probe?
Because every use case is different, there is no set schedule for recalibration.
If you are using your probe in a fish tank, a hydroponic system or any environment that has
generally weak levels of chemical reactions you will only need to recalibrate your probe
once per year for the first 2 years. After that every ~6 months.
If you are using the ORP probe in batch chemical manufacturing, industrial process, or
in a solution that is known to have strong chemical reactions, then calibration should be
done monthly or in extreme cases after each batch.

output a different voltage in the presence of oxygen. The only thing that is constant is that

A pH (potential of Hydrogen) probe measures the hydrogen ion activity in a liquid.
At the tip of a pH probe is a glass membrane. This glass membrane permits hydrogen
ions from the liquid being measured to defuse into the outer layer of the glass, while
larger ions remain in the solution. The difference in the concentration of hydrogen ions
(outside the probe vs. inside the probe) creates a VERY small current. This current
is proportional to the concentration of hydrogen ions in the liquid being measured.

2.3 Measurement
The solubility of oxygen in water depends on the
temperature and ionic strength of the water. The higher the
atmospheric pressure on the water’s surface and the lower the
temperature and conductivity of the water, the more oxygen
will be dissolved in the water.
Degassing, mineral precipitation, and other chemical,
physical, and biological reactions can cause the DO concentra-
tion of a water sample to change substantially within minutes
after sample collection, especially if the water sampled was
originally isolated from the atmosphere as in the case of
groundwater or water in a deep lake or reservoir.
The solubility of oxygen in water decreases as salinity
increases. Correction factors for salinity typically are applied
after measuring DO for single-point samples; however, for
DO measurements made with multiparameter instruments
that include calibrated specific-conductance sensors, it is
wise to activate the instrument’s internal salinity correction
algorithms. Information that pertains to oxygen solubility and
salinity is given in section 5.0, including the link to an online
program that generates tables of DO solubility values and
(or) salinity correction factors over a range of user-specified
temperature, atmospheric pressure, and salinity or specific
conductance (https://water.usgs.gov/software/DOTABLES/).
2.3.1 Surface Water
Standard determinations of DO in riverine surface water
represent the cross-sectional median or mean DO concentra-
tion at the time of observation.

Apart from that placement rule, you can take the readings in any sequence as long as each sensor is calibrated and allowed to equilibrate to the water temperature before recording.

turns.question: What do I need to do to the sensors in between each one so nothing carries over?
turns.answer:
To avoid any carry‑over when you move from one probe to the next, the USGS field‑measurement procedure calls for a rinse with de‑ionized water (DIW) between each sensor and, when needed, a gentle cleaning of the probe surface.

* **General rinse** – “Between calibrations and measurements of different samples, rinse the electrode and thermistor with DIW and then again with the new sample or buffer.”【18†"Between calibrations and measurements of different samples, rinse the electrode and thermistor with DIW and then again with the new sample or buffer."】

* **Conductivity probe** – Watch for bubbles and tap the probe to release them, then brush off any soft deposits. “Be sure to watch out for air bubbles… Lightly tap your conductivity probe to knock out any bubbles… Over time conductivity probes can become dirty and covered in deposits… Soft coatings can be removed by lightly brushing around the conducting area.”【8†"Be sure to watch out for air bubbles… Lightly tap your conductivity probe to knock out any bubbles… Over time conductivity probes can become dirty and covered in deposits… Soft coatings can be removed by lightly brushing around the conducting area."】

* **pH probe** – Remove any coating on the glass bulb before the next measurement. “Coating of the pH bulb can lead to erroneous readings… Soft coatings can be removed by vigorous stirring or by the use of a squirt bottle… hard coatings, should be chemically removed using a light bleach solution.”【9†"Coating of the pH bulb can lead to erroneous readings… Soft coatings can be removed by vigorous stirring or by the use of a squirt bottle… hard coatings, should be chemically removed using a light bleach solution."】

* **ORP probe** – Clean the platinum tip similarly. “Coating of the platinum tip can lead to erroneous readings… Soft coatings can be removed by vigorous stirring… hard coatings, should be chemically removed using a light bleach solution or a 5 – 10% hydrochloric acid (HCl) soak.”【9†"Coating of the platinum tip can lead to erroneous readings… Soft coatings can be removed by vigorous stirring… hard coatings, should be chemically removed using a light bleach solution or a 5 – 10% hydrochloric acid (HCl) soak."】

* **Dissolved‑oxygen probe** – Rinse and, if needed, brush the membrane and cap; a mild bleach mixture can be used for tougher fouling. “Over time, the membrane can wear out… Soft coatings can be removed by lightly brushing around the sides of the probe and membrane cap. If the probes membrane is in need of cleaning, use a mild bleach mixture.”【11†"Over time, the membrane can wear out… Soft coatings can be removed by lightly brushing around the sides of the probe and membrane cap. If the probes membrane is in need of cleaning, use a mild bleach mixture."】

**In practice:** after you finish reading one sensor, rinse it thoroughly with DIW, perform the brief cleaning appropriate to that probe (bubble removal, gentle brushing, or a quick bleach/HCl dip for stubborn films), rinse again with DIW, and keep the probe wet until you start the next measurement. This sequence prevents residues from one sensor influencing the next.

Operating principle
ORP stands for oxidation/reduction potential. Oxidation is the loss of electrons and
reduction is the gain of electrons. The output of the probe is represented in millivolts and
can be positive or negative.
Just like a pH probe measures hydrogen ion activity in a liquid; an ORP probe measures
electron activity in a liquid. The ORP readings represents how strongly electrons are
transferred to or from substances in a liquid. Keeping in mind that the readings do not
indicate the amount of electrons available for transfer.

damage, and water intrusion into the readout case. Many
digital thermometers are not water resistant or waterproof.

or intended for complete immersion. Most certified digital
thermometers are certified as a unit containing the sensor and

important to be familiar with and to follow the manufacturer’s
instructions for use and care.

sensor’s depth limit, if it has one, and compatibility
with corrosive solutions. Avoid submerging the sensor
past its depth limit or in corrosive solutions unless
compatibility is confirmed by the manufacturer.

unless the manufacturer affirms that they are water-

are part of some digital thermometers.

detergent.

be disinfected, use a weak (0.005 percent) bleach

• Do not autoclave temperature sensors (unless auto-
claving is sanctioned by the manufacturer).
• If your digital thermometer has a detachable sensor

* **pH probe** – Remove any coating on the glass bulb before the next measurement. “Coating of the pH bulb can lead to erroneous readings… Soft coatings can be removed by vigorous stirring or by the use of a squirt bottle… hard coatings, should be chemically removed using a light bleach solution.”【9†"Coating of the pH bulb can lead to erroneous readings… Soft coatings can be removed by vigorous stirring or by the use of a squirt bottle… hard coatings, should be chemically removed using a light bleach solution."】

* **ORP probe** – Clean the platinum tip similarly. “Coating of the platinum tip can lead to erroneous readings… Soft coatings can be removed by vigorous stirring… hard coatings, should be chemically removed using a light bleach solution or a 5 – 10% hydrochloric acid (HCl) soak.”【9†"Coating of the platinum tip can lead to erroneous readings… Soft coatings can be removed by vigorous stirring… hard coatings, should be chemically removed using a light bleach solution or a 5 – 10% hydrochloric acid (HCl) soak."】

* **Dissolved‑oxygen probe** – Rinse and, if needed, brush the membrane and cap; a mild bleach mixture can be used for tougher fouling. “Over time, the membrane can wear out… Soft coatings can be removed by lightly brushing around the sides of the probe and membrane cap. If the probes membrane is in need of cleaning, use a mild bleach mixture.”【11†"Over time, the membrane can wear out… Soft coatings can be removed by lightly brushing around the sides of the probe and membrane cap. If the probes membrane is in need of cleaning, use a mild bleach mixture."】

**In practice:** after you finish reading one sensor, rinse it thoroughly with DIW, perform the brief cleaning appropriate to that probe (bubble removal, gentle brushing, or a quick bleach/HCl dip for stubborn films), rinse again with DIW, and keep the probe wet until you start the next measurement. This sequence prevents residues from one sensor influencing the next.
